statement: The maximum number of real solutions over generic real input data is one, so every generic real instance is totally real.

source.version: arXiv:0906.3828v4 (18 January 2010), primary PDF reinspected 4 November 2026

scope: The generic fibre for plane quintics of genus 6 through 20 points. For real-count assertions, all prescribed points and lines (including any specified contact point) are real and satisfy the genericity assumptions.

origin.inheritance_basis: A reduced generic complex fibre of cardinality one has trivial permutation action; for generic real inputs conjugation fixes its unique solution.

notes:
Elementary deduction from the recorded complex count one. Complex conjugation preserves the fibre for real input data, so its unique point is fixed and the solution curve is defined over R. A permutation action on a singleton is trivial. These deductions are supplied here explicitly; they are not attributed as separate theorems in the cited paper. The assertion concerns real solution curves, not reality of every point on a real curve.

The numerical count is associated with the earlier recursion (Caporaso–Harris for plane curves of arbitrary genus). Fomin–Mikhalkin’s table remains the inspected verification source; their floor-diagram Theorem 1.6 explicitly restates Brugallé–Mikhalkin. This is not a claim that the individual numerical value was historically first found by the cited recursion.

Lucia Caporaso; Joe Harris, Counting plane curves of any genus (1998, article ID caporaso_1996_plane_curves). Earlier attribution or derivation. The current result cites the article actually inspected at the recorded source locator, which restates, tabulates, or specializes this earlier work.
